questions.stem: Like other fat-soluble vitamins, Vitamin A can be stored in the body and cause toxicity. Vitamin A toxicity leads to which of the following conditions?Bronze DiabetesAlopeciaLoss of appetiteEcchymotic patchesIncreased intracranial tensionSelect the correct answer from given below code:
questions.solutionHtml:
2,5

Excess of vitamin A is toxic and manifests as:

  • Raised Intracranial tension resembling Brain Tumour (Known as Pseudo Tumour Cerebri)
  • Hepatomegaly
  • Liver damage
  • Hyperlipidemia
  • Blurred Vision
  • Alopecia
  • Dry pruritic skin
  • Ecchymotic patches appear due to Vitamin K deficiency
  • Bronze Diabetes occurs as a result of iron overload.
  • Loss of appetite generally occurs as a result of vitamin D toxicity.



Harper's, Illustrated Biochemistry: 32nd Edition, Page No. 538

questions.stem: A teenager is presented with severe cystic acne. The patient is prescribed Isotretinoin. Chemically isotretinoin is:
questions.solutionHtml:
13 cis-retinoic acid

Isotretinoin is a synthetic retinoid, i.e., 13 cis retinoic acid

uses:

  • Acne vulgaris
  • Oral leukoplakia
  • Pityriasis rubra pilaris

Side effects:

  • Alopecia
  • Tendon rupture/tendinitis
  • Elevation of Lipoprotein (a)
  • Teratogenicity

Extra Information:

All-trans retinoic acid is involved in cell differentiation.

  • All-trans retinoic acid binds to nuclear receptors (retinoic acid receptors).
  • The activated retinoic acid-receptor complex interacts with response elements on the DNA and regulates the transcription of specific genes in different tissues.
  • Ex: Control of expression of keratin gene in epithelial tissues.

NOTE: All-trans retinoic acid (ATRA) treats acute promyelocytic leukemia.

questions.stem: A child of age six years was brought to the pediatric department. A patient complained of pain in the legs past six months. Upon examination, a bowing deformity was reported in the patient's lower extremities. The X-ray investigation of the legs revealed bowing of tibiae and widening of epiphyses. Bone mineral density was normal. Deficiency of which vitamin is responsible for the above manifestations?
questions.solutionHtml:
Vitamin D
Vitamin D is essential for the mineralization of bones. Its deficiency results in bone deformities in children called rickets.

questions.stem: A newborn baby of 7 days of age was taken to the hospital's emergency ward. The baby was bleeding. After examination, the prothrombin time was reduced to below 50% of the normal value. No other abnormality was detected. Select the correct statement that describes the condition.

options.label: B
options.text: Newborn infant with low levels of vitamin K

questions.solutionHtml:
All of the above
Newborn babies suffer from a deficiency of vitamin K. It can be early onset within 24 h of birth infants, Classic bleeding within the first week after birth, and Late-onset bleeding within six months after childbirth.

questions.stem: Vitamin E family consists of tocopherols and tocotrienols with four vitamers α, β, γ, and δ in each group. They have powerful biological antioxidant activity, which differs among these forms. Which of the following tocopherol is the most active form of vitamin E?
questions.solutionHtml:
Alpha
  • α-tocopherol is the most active form.
  • It is also a form of vitamin E preferentially absorbed and accumulated in humans.
  • Look at the isoprene side chain of tocopherol. All fat-soluble vitamins contain isoprene units.

Structure of alpha-tocopherol.

questions.stem: Pyridoxine (vitamin B6) deficiencies are generally associated with microcytic, hypochromic anemia. Why does vitamin B6 deficiency result in small (microcytic), pale (hypochromic) RBCs?
questions.solutionHtml:
ALA synthase is affected
  • ALA synthase catalyzes the first and rate-limiting step of heme synthesis.
  • PLP (Vitamin B6) is necessary for this reaction.
  • That is why in B6 deficiency, the hemoglobin synthesis is low, resulting in small size and hypochromic RBCs leading to microcytic and hypochromic anemia.





Harper's, Illustrated Biochemistry: 32nd Edition, Page No. 543

questions.stem: Pyridoxal phosphate (PLP) is synthesized from the vitamin pyridoxine (vitamin B6) and is a cofactor of various reactions. The reactive aldehyde group of PLP usually is a part of covalent catalysis for these enzyme-catalyzed reactions. PLP is required for the activity of all of the following enzymes except:
questions.solutionHtml:
Glucose 6 phosphate dehydrogenase

Vitamin B6 is involved in a variety of reactions, as shown below:

  • Carbohydrate metabolism: Glycogen Phosphorylase
  • Amino Acid Metabolism: All Transaminases – ALT, AST Cystathionine β-synthase, Cystathioninase, decarboxylases, Kynureninase, Heme synthesis, ALA synthase
  • Lipid metabolism: Synthesis of arachidonic acid, Synthesis of Sphingosine (Serine palmitoyltransferase & sphingosine-1-phosphate lyase)
  • Steroid Hormone Action: Removes hormone receptor complex from DNA & terminates the hormone's action.

Glucose 6 phosphate dehydrogenase requires NADP or vitamin B3 (Niacin) as a coenzyme.





Harper's, Illustrated Biochemistry: 32nd Edition, Page No. 543

questions.stem: Dietary antioxidants (e.g., vitamins, carotenoids, flavonoids) and endogenously produced free-radical scavengers have a common structural feature, a conjugated double-bond system such as an aromatic ring. All of the following vitamins are antioxidants EXCEPT:
questions.solutionHtml:
Vitamin K
  • Remember the antioxidant vitamins by the mnemonic ACE or CEA. Note that it is the β carotene form of Vitamin A.
  • β-carotene and vitamin E are lipid phase anti-oxidant.
  • Vitamin C is an aqueous phase antioxidant.
  • Extra Edge: Vitamin E is a chain-breaking antioxidant.

questions.stem: Select the TRUE statement about vitamin B12:

options.label: A
options.text: Does not act as a cofactor

options.label: B
options.text: Involved in the transfer of amino groups

options.label: C
options.text: Requires a specific glycoprotein for its absorption

options.label: D
options.text: Dietary requirement is met by intake of plant products

questions.answerText: Requires a specific glycoprotein for its absorption
questions.solutionHtml:
Requires a specific glycoprotein for its absorption

Option analysis:

  • Methyl cobalamine and 5'-deoxy adenosyl cobalamine are the coenzyme forms of vitamin B12 → option a is excluded.
  • Vitamin B6 is involved in the transfer of amino groups, not B12 → option b is excluded.
  • Dietary source (milk, curd, cheese, egg, liver, meat, fish) of B12 is exclusive of animal origin, and no plant source of vitamin B12 → option d is excluded.
  • Intrinsic factor (IF), an intrinsic gastric factor (GIF), is a glycoprotein produced by the stomach's parietal cells. It is necessary to absorb B12 in the ileum →, so option c is the answer.




Harper's, Illustrated Biochemistry: 32nd Edition, Page No. 544

questions.stem: A 20-month-old male infant presented with developmental delay, seizures, and eczema. His urine has a characteristic tom cat smell, and blood analysis indicated organic acidemia. The patient is advised to take biotin supplementation to treat which of the following conditions?
questions.solutionHtml:
Multiple carboxylase deficiency

Multiple carboxylase/biotinidase deficiency:

  • Autosomal recessive disorder due to a defect in Holocarboxylase synthase or biotinidase deficiency.
  • These are required to generate the active form of biotin needed for carboxylation reactions (see Fig)

Clinical features:

  • Metabolic ketoacidosis
  • Diffuse rash
  • Alopecia
  • Seizures
  • Intellectual disability

questions.stem: Many drugs are used as rescue therapy for preventing the adverse effects of anticancer drugs. One such drug, Folinic acid, is used during methotrexate therapy. Chemically, Folinic acid is which one of the following compounds?
questions.solutionHtml:
5-formyl tetrahydrofolate
  • Folinic acid is 5-formyltetrahydrofolate. It is also known as leucovorin and citrovorum factor.
  • Folinic acid can be directly converted to N5, N10-methylene tetrahydrofolate.

questions.stem: Which vitamin deficiency is associated with progressive keratinization of the cornea?
questions.solutionHtml:
Vitamin A
  • Vitamin A deficiency is the most important preventable cause of blindness.
  • The earliest sign of deficiency is a loss of sensitivity to green light →, followed by impairment to adapt to dim light →, then night blindness (inability to see in the dark)
  • More prolonged deficiency leads to xerophthalmia: keratinization of the cornea and blindness.




Harper's, Illustrated Biochemistry: 32nd Edition, Page No. 538

questions.stem: Wernicke encephalopathy is due to acute dietary deficiency of
questions.solutionHtml:
Thiamine

Wernicke’s (ophthalmoparesis, ataxia, and encephalopathy) and Korsakoff’s (retrograde and anterograde amnesia) syndrome is common in alcoholics due to thiamine deficiency.

Pathogenesis:

  • Thiamine is needed for oxidative decarboxylation reactions (pyruvate dehydrogenase and α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase) that are very important for glucose metabolism.
  • Thiamine deficiency produces a diffuse decrease in cerebral glucose utilization and results in mitochondrial damage.
  • Glutamate accumulates due to impairment of α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase activity and, in combination with the energy deficiency, may result in excitotoxic cell damage.




Harper's, Illustrated Biochemistry: 32nd Edition, Page No. 541-542

questions.stem: A patient with biliary atresia is more prone to a deficiency of
questions.solutionHtml:
Vit K

Biliary atresia leads to malabsorption of fat-soluble vitamins

This is an indirect question.

  • Bile is needed for the digestion of lipids (micelle formation)
  • Absence of bile leads to lipid malabsorption
  • Lipid soluble vitamins are absorbed along with lipids
  • Among the options, Vitamin K is the only fat-soluble vitamin. So, it is the answer.
  • Moreover, the Absorption of carotenes and fat-soluble vitamins is impaired on a very low-fat diet.

questions.stem: An overweight person goes on a high-carbohydrate and low-fat diet to lose body fat. To metabolize these excess carbohydrates, he has to increase the RDA level of which of the following vitamins?
questions.solutionHtml:
Thiamine
  • Thiamine is needed for only four enzymes in the body. They are:-
    • Pyruvate dehydrogenase
    • α ketoglutarate dehydrogenase
    • Transketolase
    • Branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase.
  • Branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase is involved in the metabolism of amino acids
  • Rest all three enzymes are involved in carbohydrate metabolism.
  • So, increased carbohydrate intake increases the requirement for thiamine also.
  • Transketolase enzyme estimation is used in thiamine deficiency




Harper's, Illustrated Biochemistry: 32nd Edition, Page No. 541

questions.stem: In Hyperhemolytic conditions or chronic hemolysis, hemoglobin is oxidatively degraded to release free heme from ferric hemoglobin. This free heme can accelerate tissue damage by promoting peroxidative reactions and activating inflammatory cascades. Which of the following protein binds to free heme to inhibit these effects?
questions.solutionHtml:
Hemopexin

Option analysis:

Ceruloplasmin: protein for transport of copper in blood

Haptoglobin: protein produced by the liver that the body uses to clear free hemoglobin (found outside of red blood cells) from circulation

Hemosiderin: is a Brown, golden pigment made of aggregates of several ferritins. It carries higher iron content but Releases iron more slowly than ferritin.

Hemopexin: is a β1-globulin that binds free heme and inhibits its deleterious oxidative effects.





Harper's, Illustrated Biochemistry: 32nd Edition, Page No. 638

questions.stem: Which of the following is true regarding anemia of chronic kidney disease?
questions.solutionHtml:
Due to erythropoietin deficiency

The anemia associated with CKD (chronic kidney disease) is:

  • Normocytic: Size of RBCs is normal- no microcytic anemia (option 4))
  • Normochromic: concentration of hemoglobin is in the standard range, but the number of RBCs is decreased. This is due to decreased erythropoietin (option 2).

Erythropoietin (EPO) is a glycoprotein produced by the kidney and promotes the proliferation and differentiation of erythrocyte precursors in bone marrow (See fig).

Chronic kidney disease → Renal failure → Low Erythropoietin → Low RBCs count

The anemia in this condition is associated with:

  • High ferritin (intracellular iron-storage protein) presumably to keep iron stored in cells and away from pathogens (option 1).

Low serum iron level due to low transferrin (iron-binding protein in plasma), hence total iron binding capacity (TIBC) is decreased in this condition






Harper's, Illustrated Biochemistry: 32nd Edition, Page No. 638

questions.stem: Absence of which of the following enzyme in humans is responsible for the inability to synthesize ascorbic acid?
questions.solutionHtml:
L-Gulonolactone oxidase

Uronic acid pathway is an alternate pathway for oxidation of glucose without ATP formation.

An intermediate (L-gluconate) of this pathway can synthesize ascorbic acid in plants by the enzyme L-gluconolactone oxidase.

However, ascorbic acid cannot be synthesized in human beings, other primates, guinea pigs, bats, and some birds and fishes because of the absence of L-Gulonolactone oxidase.

questions.solutionHtml:
Vitamin D intoxication

Vitamin D intoxication leads to elevated plasma concentration of calcium

This can lead to contraction of blood vessels, high blood pressure, and calcinosis—the calcification of soft tissues.

Causes of hypercalcemia

Causes of hypocalcemia

●        Multiple myeloma and other osteolytic diseases

●        Metastatic carcinoma of bone

●        Thiazide diuretics

●        Vitamin D intoxication

●        Hypoparathyroidism

questions.stem: A man has mild liver disease, arthritis, fatigue, and grayish skin pigmentation. Highly elevated level of iron is observed in his liver biopsy report. Which of the following conditions will be most likely in this patient?
questions.solutionHtml:
High Serum Ferritin

The diagnosis is hemochromatosis. It is an autosomal recessive disorder due to a mutation in histocompatibility region of chromosome 6. In this disease, Iron absorption is increased from the small intestine resulting in increased serum iron and iron-ferritin complex (see Fig).

As transferrin carries iron in the blood, higher transferrin saturation will be observed.

questions.stem: A woman develops anemia in 6th month of her first pregnancy. Blood work revealed hypersegmented neutrophils with increased mean cell volume (MVC), morphological alterations in other cell types, and elevated serum levels of homocysteine. Anemia in this woman is caused most likely due to:
questions.solutionHtml:
Folate deficiency

The most likely reason of this woman condition is folate deficiency.

DNA synthesis indirectly requires Folic acid (folate required for conversion of dUMP to dTMP, leading to decreased thymidine, which is required for DNA synthesis).

In Folic acid deficiency, DNA replication and, thus, cell division are affected. The cytoplasm of folate deficient cells grows at a normal rate, but cell division is delayed. So abnormally large cells are formed. This leads to megaloblastic anemia.

As Folate is required for homocysteine to methionine conversion, its deficiency will cause homocysteine accumulation in serum.

All Rapidly dividing cells, e.g. bone marrow and intestinal mucosa, are most affected.

Supplements of Folate given in appropriate doses before conception can significantly reduce the incidence of Spina Bifida and other neural tube defects.

Option b. Iron deficiency presents as microcytic, hypochromic anemia and would not elevate homocysteine.





Harper's, Illustrated Biochemistry: 32nd Edition, Page No. 545-546

questions.stem: Iron in intestinal mucosal cells or stored in the liver may be transferred into the blood for transport to other tissues by some proteins. Which of the following molecules delivers iron to tissues by binding to specific cell surface receptors?
questions.solutionHtml:
Transferrin
  • Transferrin is a β1-globulin synthesized in the liver and is the transporter of iron.

Absorption and Transport of Iron

Absorption in the intestinal cell:

  • Cytochrome b reductase one or Duodenal cytochrome b (Dcytb) is a ferric reductase enzyme that converts Fe3+ to Fe2+, and aids the entry of Fe2+ into the mucosal cell
  • The ferrous iron is then transported in the cell by a divalent metal transporter (DMT-1).
  • Divalent Metal/Cation Transporter 1(DMT1 or DCT1) is Located on the apical membrane of enterocytes. Body iron stores regulate DMT1 expression to maintain iron homeostasis.

Transport in blood:

  • For transport, ferrous iron needs to be oxidized to ferric iron. This is done by hephaestin, a membrane-associated ferroxidase protein.
  • In the blood, ceruloplasmin, a copper-containing ferroxidase, oxidizes any ferrous iron to ferric iron
  • Transferrin can carry two molecules of ferric ion. (apo transferrin + 2 Fe3+ = Holo-transferrin)
  • Transferrin delivers the iron to different tissue cells by receptor-mediated endocytosis.
  • The iron can be incorporated into various iron-containing proteins or stored in ferritin.





Harper's, Illustrated Biochemistry: 32nd Edition, Page No. 639-641

questions.stem: A 10-year-old boy presented to OPD with hepatosplenomegaly and cirrhosis. Blood and urine examinations indicated a higher-than-normal level of free copper. The eye examination showed Kayser-Fleisher (KF) rings characteristic of Wilson's hepatolenticular degeneration. Which of the following gene is defective in this disease?
questions.solutionHtml:
ATP 7A

Defects in copper metabolism:

 

Menkes disease

Wilson's disease

Defective gene & its product

ATP7A- ATPase (chromosome)

ATP7B (Chromosome 13)

Inheritance

●        X-linked recessive

●        Autosomal recessive

Pathogenic defect

●        Intestinal absorption of copper

●        Defective biliary excretion of copper

●        Accumulation of copper in liver

●        Spillage into circulation due to liver damage

Blood and urinary copper

↓

↑

Clinical features

●        Kinky hair and those of copper deficiency

●        Kayser-Fleischer ring in cornea

●        Liver cirrhosis

●        Neurological manifestations

NOTE: Menkes is caused by defective lysyl oxidase enzyme, This results from a deficiency of its co-factor, i.e., copper due to a defect in the ATP7A gene.





Harper's, Illustrated Biochemistry: 32nd Edition, Page No. 641

questions.stem: Which of the following mineral is a major component of biological membranes?
questions.solutionHtml:
Phosphorus
  • Lipid bilayer is made up of phospholipids- Lecithin, Sphingomyelin, Phosphatidyl Inositol, and Phosphatidyl serine.
  • So, phosphorus is a major component of biological membranes.





Harper's, Illustrated Biochemistry: 32nd Edition, Page No. 209-210

questions.stem: Vitamin E is the most widely distributed antioxidant in nature and protects cells from oxidative stress due to reactive oxygen species. Which of the following mineral has a similar action to vitamin E?
questions.solutionHtml:
Selenium
  • Selenium is needed for the enzyme glutathione peroxidase involved in the defense against free radical-mediated damage of lipid bilayer
  • Vitamin E is also involved in the same
  • So, selenium has a sparing effect on Vitamin E, i.e. Vitamin E deficiency can be corrected with selenium and vice versa.





Harper's, Illustrated Biochemistry: 32nd Edition, Page No. 554

questions.stem: Uncontrolled phagocytosis of oxidized LDL particles is a major stimulus for developing foam cells and fatty streaks in the vascular subendothelium. This process may be inhibited by increased dietary intake of
questions.solutionHtml:
vitamin E
  • Oxidation of lipid and protein portion of LDL is deleterious
  • Oxidised LDL is taken up by scavenger receptors of the macrophages and leads to foam cell formation. This promotes atherosclerosis. Thus, it is important to prevent the oxidation of LDL.
  • Vitamin E is the chain-breaking antioxidant that acts on the lipid phase of LDL and prevents lipid peroxidation.
  • Other chain-breaking antioxidants are Vit A, C; SOD, and Uric acid
  • Preventive antioxidants are glutathione peroxidase, and catalase





Harper's, Illustrated Biochemistry: 32nd Edition, Page No. 540

questions.stem: Biotin, also called vitamin B7, is involved in a wide range of metabolic processes, primarily related to using fats, carbohydrates, and amino acids. Which of the following processes does not require this vitamin?

options.label: D
options.text: Propionyl CoA to Methyl Malonyl CoA

questions.solutionHtml:
Glutamate to GABA

Biotin (Vitamin B7) is required mainly in carboxylation reactions

  • Acetyl CoA to Malonyl CoA is done by enzyme Acetyl CoA carboxylase.
  • Pyruvate to Oxaloacetate is done by the enzyme Pyruvate carboxylase.
  • Propionyl CoA to Methyl Malonyl CoA is done by the enzyme Propionyl CoA carboxylase.
  • Glutamate to GABA conversion is a simple decarboxylation reaction requiring vitamin B6, i.e., Pyridoxine.




Satyanarayana's Biochemistry, 5th edition page no. 146-151

questions.stem: Histidine decarboxylase is an enzyme involved in the decarboxylation of histidine amino acid into a pharmacological amine, histamine. In humans, histamine is a significant biogenic amine. It is important as a neurotransmitter in controlling neurotransmission, gastric acid secretion, and immunity. Histidine decarboxylase is the sole enzyme in a single-step reaction. Name the vitamin whose derivative is covalently attached to histidine decarboxylase?
questions.solutionHtml:
Pyridoxine

Histidine decarboxylase decarboxylates histidine via the coenzyme pyridoxal phosphate. It is the primary biological source of histamine. Histamine is a vital biogenic amine that moderates numerous physiologic processes.





Harper's, Illustrated Biochemistry, 31st Edition, Page No. 308

questions.stem: A 60-year-old woman was severely malnourished and developed macrocytic anemia. Her blood and urine analysis further revealed elevated levels of homocysteine and methylmalonate. The leucocyte transketolase levels were also below normal levels. What symptoms out of the following confirm that the anemia in this woman is due to a primary deficiency of cyanocobalamin (B12)?
questions.solutionHtml:
Elevated methylmalonate

Macrocytic anemia: RBC's are more significant than their normal size

Macrocytic anemia and elevated homocysteine, both can be caused by either B12 or folate deficiency.

However, methyl malonyl CoA mutase specifically requires B12 and not folate for activity.

  • MMA is elevated in 90–98% of patients with B12 However, it is an acute condition but not a specific condition.
  • The coenzyme form of B12,e., Adenosyl cobalamine, is required for the activity of methyl malonyl-CoA mutase, which covert methyl malonyl-CoA into succinyl-CoA (See figure).
  • Due to deficiency of B12, methyl malonyl may accumulate, causing malonyl aciduria (See fig below).






Harper's, Illustrated Biochemistry: 32nd Edition, Page No. 544

questions.stem: Antioxidant defense enzymes, free-radical scavengers, cellular compartmentalization, metal sequestration, and repairing damaged cellular components counter oxygen toxicity in the form of reactive oxygen species. All of the following minerals can act as a natural-antioxidants except.
questions.solutionHtml:
Iron

Zn plays a role as an anti-oxidant as it binds with the SH group of biomolecules protecting them from oxidation. Also, it increases the activation of anti-oxidant properties.

Action of Se is complementary to Vitamin E, a constituent of Glutathione Peroxidase and Selenocysteine.

Cu has a role as an anti-oxidant as it is present as a constituent in Cu/Zn SOD and Ceruloplasmin.

Biological Functions of Iron:

  • Transport and storage of O2 (Hb and Mb) and CO2.
  • In ETC as a component of cytochromes.
  • Co-factor for many enzymes,g., Catalase, Peroxidase, Tryptophan Pyrrolase
  • Role in phagocytosis (Peroxidase contains iron required for Phagocytosis).




Harper's, Illustrated Biochemistry: 32nd Edition, Page No. 564

questions.stem: A patient presented in OPD with symptoms of Beri-Beri, such as psychosis, confabulations, progressive muscle wasting, etc., induced by Thiamine deficiency. The physician can trace the origin of his symptoms to all of the following conditions except

options.label: D
options.text: Chronic heart failure patient on diuretics

questions.solutionHtml:
Homocystinuria

Homocystinuria (Option B) occurs due to deficiency of vitamins – B6, B9 & B12 (NOT Vitamin B1, i.e., Thiamine).





Harper's, Illustrated Biochemistry: 32nd Edition, Page No. 540-541

questions.stem: Three different forms of vitamin D namely Cholecalciferol (D3), 1, 25 (OH)2 D3, and 25-OH D3, are produced as intermediates during the biosynthesis of vitamin D. The active form 1,25 (OH)2 Cholecalciferol or calcitriol is formed in which of following organs?
questions.solutionHtml:
Kidney

Synthesis of Vitamin D:

  • Activation of 7-dehydro cholesterol by UV light in the skin produces Cholecalciferol
  • 25-hydroxylation in the liver to form 25-hydroxy cholecalciferol
  • 1-alpha- hydroxylation in kidneys to form 1,25 dihydroxy cholecalciferol
  • PTH activates 1-alpha hydroxylase of kidneys
So, 25-hydroxy Cholecalciferol is formed in liver Whereas 1, 25 (OH)2 Cholecalciferol is formed in kidneys.




Harper's, Illustrated Biochemistry: 32nd Edition, Page No. 538-539

questions.stem: Vitamins synthesized by human enzymes during metabolism are called as Atypical vitamins and do not include vitamins synthesized by intestinal microflora. Which of the following vitamin is synthesized by intestinal bacteria?
questions.solutionHtml:
Vitamin K
  • Vitamins that are synthesized by intestinal flora are Vitamin B2, B5, B7 & Vitamin K.
  • Vitamin B3 and Vitamin D are two vitamins that are synthesized by the human body. So these are called Atypical Vitamins. These vitamins are synthesized by human enzymes during metabolism, not by intestinal bacterial enzymes.
  • Vitamin B3 is synthesized from Tryptophan
  • Vitamin D is synthesized from 7-Dehydro Cholesterol by UV light in the skin.



Harper's, Illustrated Biochemistry: 32nd Edition, Page No. 540

questions.stem: Vitamin E deficiency is rare in healthy people but can occur in patients with diseases related to poor fat digestion and absorption. Vitamin E deficiency can cause all of the following symptoms EXCEPT:
questions.solutionHtml:
Megaloblastic anemia

 

Deficiency of vitamin E can lead to:

  • Neurological problems
    • Difficulty coordinating movements (ataxia)
    • Speech (dysarthria)
    • Loss of reflexes in the legs (lower limb areflexia)
    • Loss of sensation in the extremities (peripheral neuropathy).
  • Ophthalmoplegia in susceptible persons.




Harper's, Illustrated Biochemistry: 32nd Edition, Page No. 540

questions.stem: Vitamins serve diverse biochemical functions such as antioxidants, growth and tissue differentiation, and hormonal and coenzymes for various metabolic enzymes. Which of the following vitamin perform its role by acting on intranuclear receptors?
questions.solutionHtml:
Vitamin D
  • Vitamin D is considered as a hormone as it is synthesized in the body, released in circulation.
  • Its primary function is regulating calcium absorption and homeostasis; the action is mediated by binding to nuclear receptors to control gene expression of genes involved in calcium metabolism.
  • In that way, the Mechanism of action of vitamin D resembles group II hormones, i.e., it binds with nuclear receptors.




Harper's, Illustrated Biochemistry: 32nd Edition, Page No. 538

questions.stem: A patient is presented with symptoms of peripheral neuropathy, which are getting worsened gradually. Blood examination revealed larger than normal RBCs. Which of the following is the best treatment which can be given to help alleviate these symptoms?
questions.solutionHtml:
Folic acid along with Hydroxycobalamin

Vitamin deficiency

Manifestation

In folate

megaloblastic anemia

B12

Megaloblastic anemia & neurological manifestations occur.

Clinical manifestations of B12 deficiency:

  • Haematological: Megaloblastic anemia, Hypersegmentation of neutrophils.
  • Neurological: Demyelination in peripheral nerves and spinal cord

Megaloblastic anemia is due to a secondary deficiency of folate (folate trap in B12 deficiency).

Peripheral neuropathy is due to the accumulation of L-methyl malonic acid.

questions.stem: Vitamin D is an atypical vitamin and can be synthesized in humans from its precursor cholesterol in the skin by exposure to UV light. Various intermediary forms of vitamin D are formed during its biosynthesis. Which of the following is the most potent form of vitamin D?
questions.solutionHtml:
1, 25- dihydroxy cholecalciferol

Vitamin D encompasses a group of sterols, which have a hormone-like function.

Bioactive vitamin D, or calcitriol, is a steroid hormone that has long been known for its important role in regulating body levels of calcium and phosphorus and in the mineralization of bone.

 

Forms of Vitamin D:

25-OH- cholecalciferol

→ Major storage and circulating form of vitamin D

●        In clinical laboratory, we measure 25-(OH) cholecalciferol.

→ aka Calcitriol

→ most biologically active form of vitamin D

questions.stemHtml: A 38-year-old female patient was on Isoniazid therapy for tuberculosis. She developed rashes on the exposed parts of her body. She has disoriented memory. Family members give a history of diarrhea also. What is the diagnosis:

options.label: D
options.text: Some other drug has caused this

questions.solutionHtml:
Niacin deficiency
  • Patient is showing Casal's Necklace and symptoms of Pellagra such Dermatitis, Dementia, Diarrhea
  • Prolonged treatment with isoniazid leads to pyridoxine deficiency, which is required for endogenous synthesis of niacin so that the patient will develop pellagra.

Etiology:

  • Dietary deficiency of nicotinic acid or its precursor tryptophan.
  • People with a staple diet of maize and Jowar. Maize is a poor source of nicotinic acid and tryptophan, and a part of nicotinic acid is in a bound form that is not assimilated in GIT. Jowar has a high content of leucine. The imbalance between leucine and other related amino acids interferes with the conversion of tryptophan to nicotinic acid.
  • Malabsorption
  • Drugs like INH, 5FU, and 6-mercaptopurine.
  • Carcinoid syndrome

T/t:

  • Niacinamide 300-500 mg/day orally in divided doses.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old male visited his dentist to consult about his loosening of teeth. A more detailed check-up reveals his gums are swollen, purple, and spongy. Physical examination revealed multiple splinter hemorrhages near the distal ends of the nail on the patient’s fingers, and wound healing is not proper in this patient. Is the patient showing deficiency symptoms?
questions.solutionHtml:
Vitamin C

Vitamin C acts as a cofactor for the enzyme lysyl and prolyl hydroxylase which is necessary for post-translation modification of collagen by hydroxylating the proline and lysine residue.

  • These hydroxylated residues are necessary for hydrogen bonding between collagen chains, strengthening collagen fibers.
  • Vitamin C deficiency leads to defective post-translational modification of collagen → loss of tensile strength of blood vessels leading to:
    • Bleeding gums
    • Ecchymoses
    • Easy disability
    • Poor wound healing (Features of scurvy).

questions.answerText: Assertion and Reason are independently true/correct statements, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion
questions.solutionHtml:
Assertion and Reason are independently true/correct statements, and Reason is the correct explanation for Assertion

questions.stemHtml: A 2-year-old child is presented with mental retardation, hypotonia, and growth retardation. Physical examination revealed depigmented grey and brittle kinky hair. Blood and urine examinations showed a lower Cu level than usual. Which of the following enzyme is affected in this patient?
questions.solutionHtml:
Lysyl oxidase

The diagnosis is Menke’s Disease

 

Menke Disease:

  • XR disease due to Cu deficiency
  • Deficient production of Cu binding P-type ATPase ATP7A in the intestine (Cu stays in intestinal cell, unable to enter blood)

C/F

  • ↓ Cu in blood and urine,
  • ↓ cp (ceruloplasmin)
  • Mental retardation, hypotonia, growth retardation, and premature birth
  • Presents in infancy, death usually by three years
  • As tyrosinase is affected which forms melanin so the patient has grey depigmented hair

questions.stem: WHO recommends the administration of zinc along with new low-osmolarity oral rehydration solutions/salts (ORS) to treat diarrhea in children up to three months of age. The use of zinc in diarrhea is because it:

options.label: A
options.text: Reduces the risk, duration, and severity of diarrheal episodes

options.label: C
options.text: Regulates intestinal transport & absorption of water and electrolytes

questions.solutionHtml:
All of the above

Zinc deficiency:

  • Increased risk of gastrointestinal infections
  • Adverse effects on the structure and function of the gastrointestinal tract
  • Impaired immune function
  • Disease is known as Acrodermatitis enteropathica

Acrodermatitis enteropathica

  • It is an autosomal recessive disease due to a defect in zinc absorbing transmembrane protein.

Symptoms:

  • Growth retardation
  • Diarrhea
  • Alopecia
  • Dermatitis around the orifices
  • Gonadal atrophy
  • Impaired wound healing

Zinc acts as a cofactor for:

  • Carbonic anhydrase
  • Carboxypeptidase
  • Lactate dehydrogenase
  • Alcohol dehydrogenase
  • Alkaline phosphatase

questions.stemHtml: A patient presented in the OPD complaining of tingling sensations in their hand and feeling weak for the past few days. He was a vegetarian but did not eat a proper diet for some time. A thorough clinical examination showed the patient also had a red, softened tongue and roughed lips. The physician suspected a vitamin deficiency and ordered which of the following enzyme assay to detect this vitamin deficiency in this patient?Which of the following enzyme assay would you perform to detect the deficiency in the child?
questions.solutionHtml:
Glutathione reductase

These are the typical presentation of riboflavin deficiency. The glutathione reductase activity test and marker enzyme for riboflavin deficiency, as this enzyme needs FAD as a prosthetic group.

Symptoms of B2 deficiency:

  • Corneal vascularization- earliest sign of deficiency.
  • Glossitis– inflammation of the tongue (magenta tongue- characteristic),
  • Cheilosis– redness and shiny appearance of lips.
  • Angular stomatitis- lesions at the mucocutaneous junction at corners of the mouth, leading to painful fissures.
  • Seborrhoeic dermatitis– rough, scaly skin because of desquamation.

questions.stem: A 14-month-old infant is presented with dilated cardiomyopathy, hypothyroidism, inability to gain weight, and failure to thrive and is diagnosed with Keshan’s cardiomyopathy. Which of the following mineral supplements can help improve this child's condition?
questions.solutionHtml:
Selenium
  • Selenium as selenocysteine is an essential component of the enzyme glutathione peroxidase
  • Selenium containing enzyme 5'-deiodinase converts thyroxine (T4) to triiodothyronine in the thyroid gland.
  • Thioredoxin reductase, involved in purine nucleotide metabolism

Sources- seafood and meat, nuts

Deficiency – Keshan’s disease

C/f:

  • Endemic Cardiomyopathy (endemic to a province of China due to soil poor in Se)
  • Muscular weakness and muscular dystrophy
  • Inability to gain weight
  • Hypothyroidism
  • hypertension
  • Eczema
  • increased risk of stroke and even cancer

Extra information:

  • Toxicity – selenium toxicity lead to Selenosis.
  • Clinical features are an emotional disturbance, diarrhea, hair loss, garlic odor (due to dimethyl selenide) in breath

questions.stem: A patient undergoing warfarin therapy for thrombotic disorders will have decreased γ-carboxyglutamate residues on which of the following coagulation factors?
questions.solutionHtml:
Factor II
  • Vitamin K is the cofactor for γ-carboxylation of glutamate residues of the proteins to produce γ- carboxy glutamate.
  • Clotting factors contain 4 to 6 γ-carboxyglutamate residues.
  • The clotting factors 2,7, 9, and 10 are activated by vitamin K-assisted carboxylation as a part of the vitamin K cycle.
  • Drug warfarin interferes with the recycling of vitamin K (see Fig).
  • Hydroquinone form of Vitamin K activates a glutamate residue in the protein substrate to a carbanion, which reacts nonenzymatically with carbon dioxide to form γ-carboxyglutamate.
  • Vitamin K epoxide is reduced to quinone by an epoxide reductase, and the quinone is reduced to the active hydroquinone by Vitamin K reductase.
  • Dicumarol & warfarin inhibits the enzyme (reductase) that converts epoxide to active Vitamin K (hydroquinone).

Hence all of the factors mentioned above will have decreased carboxy glutamate residues in patient taking warfarin.

questions.stem: Vitamins of vitamin A are precursors for synthesizing the active forms of vitamin A and are found sufficiently in plant-based vegetarian diets. The most abundant form of dietary provitamin A is
questions.solutionHtml:

Carotenoids are provitamins of vitamin A which are present in plants.

questions.stem: A 20-year-old alcoholic malnourished patient presented to the hospital with respiratory distress. His pulse was 112 / minute. The patient had edema, hypertension, and systolic murmur along the left sternal edge. Bilateral crepitations were felt in the lungs. A diagnosis of congestive high-output cardiac failure was made. The physician suspected thiamine deficiency. Which of the following test will most likely support the diagnosis:
questions.solutionHtml:
Erythrocyte transketolase activity

Chronic alcoholics are at risk for thiamine deficiency, This is a case of Wet/cardiacBeri-Beri, i.e., Vitamin B1deficiency. Vitamin B1 is mainly involved in Oxidative Decarboxylation reactions, so in B1deficiency, highly aerobic tissues, e.g., the heart and brain, fail first.

Thiamine (vitamin B1) Deficiency

  • It is assessed by Erythrocyte transketolase activity.
  • Thiamine (Vitamin B1) is the marker for transketolase enzyme →which is involved in the HMP pathway (in RBCs)
  • Activity of Transketolase is measured (not the quantity).
  • No importance of checking serum thiamine

Riboflavin (Vitamin B2) Deficiency

RBC glutathione reductase is the marker for vitamin B2 deficiency.





Harper's, Illustrated Biochemistry: 32nd Edition, Page No. 541-542

questions.stem: After consuming raw eggs, a person presents with weakness, fatigue & hypoglycemia. The doctor gave him vitamin tablets. Which enzyme deficiency is causing hypoglycemia in this patient:
questions.solutionHtml:
Pyruvate carboxylase
  • Excess consumption of raw eggs, which contains a protein ‘avidin’→ tightly binds to Biotin (Vit B7) and is excreted along with biotin leading to biotin deficiency
  • Biotin is required for all carboxylases.
  • All carboxylases require ATP, also
  • So, the enzyme affected is carboxylase which requires Biotin as a coenzyme
  • When cooked, avidin is partially denatured, and its binding to biotin is reduced. So cooked egg whites are safe to consume.

Pyruvate Carboxylase is the first enzyme of gluconeogenesis.

Regarding other options:

Glycogen Phosphorylase

  • ROLE of Glycogenolysis
  • Requires vitamin B6 (Pyridoxal phosphate)
  • No relation with glycogen phosphorylase and egg avidin

Glucose 6 phosphatase

  • A common enzyme in gluconeogenesis and glycogenolysis
  • Deficiency leads to hypoglycemia, and that is called Von Gierke’s disease (Type 1 glycogen storage disease).

- Von Gierke’s disease is the most common glycogen storage disease, especially in children.





Harper's, Illustrated Biochemistry: 32nd Edition, Page No. 546

questions.stem: A 15-month-old child is brought to a hospital for severe dialarhoea and dermatitis. She is also low in weight for her age. Physical examination shows the rash is not typical of yeast infection. It is distributed beyond the genital area and is prevalent on knees and tissue around the mouth and anus. She also has swelling of the hands and feet (edema) and has lost her hair. Which one of the following minerals supplements can most help relieve her symptoms?
questions.solutionHtml:
Zinc
  • The infant is suffering from Acrodermatitis enteropathica that is a rare autosomal recessive disorder characterized by abnormalities in zinc absorption.
  • It is characterized by simultaneous skin inflammation (Dermatitis) and Diarrhoea. The skin on cheeks, elbows, knees, and tissue around the mouth and anus is inflamed.
  • Administration of zinc and new low-osmolarity oral rehydration solutions/salts (ORS) can reduce diarrheal episodes' risk, duration, and severity for up to three months.
  • Minerals are essential for enzyme reactions (cofactors are distinguished from coenzymes that function in group transfer and undergo chemical reactions), including cobalt, copper, iron, molybdenum, selenium, and zinc. Examples include copper in cytochrome oxidase, iron in all the cytochromes, magnesium for all enzymes utilizing ATP, and zinc in lactate dehydrogenase.
  • Arsenic, lead, and antimony cause disease when present in excess.



Devlin Textbook of Biochemistry with clinical correlations 7th edition page no. 1091-1092

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man presents to his physician complaining of tenderness, aching of bone, and generalized muscle weakness. On consultation, it is evident that he has a very sedentary lifestyle, with most of his time spent watching television in his room. He also reports a poor diet, mostly devoid of fresh fruits and vegetables. A carpal spasm is noted after the cuff is inflated while taking the patient's blood pressure. Radiographs showed reduced bone density. Which of the following laboratory abnormalities would also be expected in this patient?
questions.solutionHtml:
Elevated parathyroid hormone
  • This patient is most probably suffering from vitamin D deficiency and osteomalacia looking at the symptoms of his poor diet and indoor lifestyle. On the radiographic exam, osteomalacia can manifest with bone pain, muscle weakness, and reduced bone density.
  • Vitamin D can be consumed from plants (ergocalciferol) or formed in sun-exposed skin (cholecalciferol). The active form of vitamin D is 1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol (calcitriol), produced in the kidney by the enzyme 1α-hydroxylase (See vitamin D biosynthesis figure in text).
  • Calcium homeostasis in the body is maintained by the interplay of calcitonin and parathyroid (PTH) hormones (refer to Fig).





Lehninger Principles of Biochemistry 6th edition Page no. 935

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man presents to the physician because of lethargy, generalized weakness, and shortness of breath for several months. He is otherwise healthy and is not taking any medication. He looks pale on physical exam, and the capillary refill is delayed. Laboratory tests reveal a hematocrit of 25% and a mean corpuscular volume of 110 fL. What is the most likely cause of her abnormal laboratory findings?
questions.solutionHtml:
Pernicious anemia
  • Pernicious anemia describes a disease in which the body cannot absorb vitamin B12. Vitamin B12 deficiency can result in megaloblastic anemia, characterized by increased mean corpuscular volume (macrocytosis), hyper-segmented neutrophils, and peripheral neuropathy.
  • The presence of neurologic symptoms led to the term “pernicious anemia” because they are progressive and eventually irreversible. The absorption of vitamin B12 from the intestine requires a binding protein called intrinsic factor that is secreted by the gastric mucosa and absorbed in the ileum.
  • A deficiency of the intrinsic factor causes pernicious anemia. Pernicious anemia can result from gastric atrophy at older ages or, more rarely, from mutations affecting the intrinsic factor itself that is present in childhood. I
  • inability to absorb vitamin B12 from the gastrointestinal tract causes more severe deficiency than nutritional deprivation in vegetarian diets. The intrinsic factor may also be diminished by autoantibodies in autoimmune diseases such as diabetes mellitus or Grave’s disease (hyperthyroidism).
  • Clinical signs of pernicious anemia may not appear until 3 to 5 years following the onset of vitamin B 12 deficiency, and the neurologic signs may occur without apparent anemia.




Harper's, Illustrated Biochemistry: 32nd Edition, Page No. 544

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man was hospitalized 30 days after his allogeneic stem cell transplant due to graft-versus-host disease and was immediately put on intravenous levofloxacin treatment. During an intravenous exchange, oozing of blood was noted from his venous access site. Laboratory examination of blood clotting tests reveals an average platelet count but prolonged prothrombin and partial thromboplastin time. A deficiency in the function of which of the following coagulation factors is the most likely cause of this patient's abnormal laboratory tests?
questions.solutionHtml:
Factor II

The long-term antibiotic treatment has caused vitamin K deficiency in this patient due to clearing of intestinal microflora, which is required for the synthesis of Vitamin K. Vitamin K is a necessary cofactor for hepatic production and activity of clotting factors II, VII, IX, and X, and proteins C and S. Factor II (prothrombin) deficiency would result in prolongation of prothrombin time and partial thromboplastin time.





Harper's, Illustrated Biochemistry: 32nd Edition, Page No. 540-541

questions.stem: A 56-year-old homeless man presents to ER with increased fatigability and exertional dyspnea. Physical examination shows significant lower extremity edema and decreased sensation over the ankles and feet. Further evaluation reveals cardiac dilation and increased cardiac output. Which vitamin deficiency is most likely responsible for this patient’s symptoms?
questions.solutionHtml:
Vitamin B1
  • Thiamin Deficiency Affects the Nervous System & the Heart.
  • Thiamin deficiency can result in three distinct syndromes: chronic peripheral neuritis, beriberi, which may or may not be associated with heart failure and edema; acute pernicious (fulminating) beriberi (shoshin beriberi), in which heart failure and metabolic abnormalities predominate, without peripheral neuritis; and Wernicke encephalopathy with Korsakoff psychosis, which is associated especially with alcohol and narcotic abuse.
  • The role of thiamin diphosphate in pyruvate dehydrogenase means that in deficiency, there is an impaired conversion of pyruvate to acetyl CoA.
  • In subjects on a relatively high carbohydrate diet, this increases plasma concentrations of lactate and pyruvate, which may cause life-threatening lactic acidosis.




Harper's, Illustrated Biochemistry, 32nd Edition, Page No. 542

questions.stem: A Male patient in the age group 34 years came to the hospital. A Patient complained about numbness in hands and feet and a burning sensation. On examination, pallor was reported in the nail beds and conjunctiva. the patient gave a history the of taking the anti-tubercular drug, Isonicotinic acid hydrazide, for six months. Which statements are correct?
questions.solutionHtml:
Deficiency of Vitamin B6
  • Given patient is showing Pellagra-like symptoms which are due to deficiency of pyridoxal phosphate.
  • INH inhibits pyridoxal kinase. It is needed to phosphorylate Pyridoxine into pyridoxal 5-P leading to its deficiency in the body.
  • Another concept is INH forms complex with pyridoxine to form hydrazone. It brings about incomplete phosphorylation of pyridoxine.
  • INH inhibits the enzyme pyridoxal kinase, which is necessary for the phosphorylation of pyridoxine.
    Vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) supplementation during isoniazid (INH) therapy is necessary for some patients to prevent the development of peripheral neuropathy.
  • As Vit. B6 (PLP) is required for Niacin synthesis from tryptophan. Hence Isoniazid therapy also causes Niacin deficiency.



Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry, 7th Edition, Page No. 382,3961—3971
